florida/brevard.intro: Brevard is one of the cheaper counties in this directory to launch in: most county park ramps on the Indian River and Banana River are free, and the fees you will meet belong to the federal sites and the port, not the county. The one county exception is the campground ramp at Long Point Park in Melbourne Beach, where non-campers buy a launch pass.
notes: Free ramps are the norm here. The county's own park pages list free parking at Lake Washington Park and P.O.W./M.I.A. Park in Melbourne, both with two-lane ramps, and the FWC inventory records no fee at Melbourne's Claude Edge Front Street Park ramp, Lee Wenner Park in Cocoa, or Scottsmoor Landing in Mims. The trade-off is space: several are one or two-lane ramps whose lots fill early on weekend mornings.

Fees do apply at the federal ramps inside the county. Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge launches such as Bairs Cove charge a refuge fee of about $10, and the Playalinda ramp at Canaveral National Seashore sits behind the seashore's per-vehicle entrance fee; the inventory records a $20 fee there. Port Canaveral and city ramps set their own charges.

In this directory, only 7 of the 77 Brevard records list a fee in the source data, and 1,167 trailer spaces are recorded. Brevard County is the most common manager, followed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.
Lagoon-side ramps can run shallow at extreme low tide. With a deeper-draft boat, plan launches and retrievals for mid or high tide rather than the bottom of the tide cycle.

florida/broward.intro: Broward's county ramps sit inside regional parks, and the only county charge is the park gate fee, which applies on weekends and holidays only. Weekday launching at a county park ramp costs nothing at the gate.
notes: Regional parks such as Markham Park, Everglades Holiday Park, West Lake Park and T.Y. Park charge $3 per vehicle (eight or fewer occupants) on weekends and holidays, and $20 per vehicle with nine or more occupants. A yearly regional park gate pass costs $30 per vehicle.

The county boating program covers ramps at Markham Park and the West Broward Boat Ramp for Everglades access, Boaters Park and West Lake Park on the Intracoastal side, and Everglades Holiday Park, a main gateway for airboat and bass fishing trips.

In this directory, 18 of the 70 Broward records list a fee in the source data, running $1 to $20. Most records are run by cities or the FWC rather than the county, and city ramps such as Fort Lauderdale's follow their own fee and parking rules.
State park ramps inside the county, like the one at Dr. Von D. Mizell-Eula Johnson State Park, charge the state park entrance fee instead of the county gate fee.

sources.label: Broward County Parks, fee schedule announcement (effective January 1, 2024)

florida/lee.intro: Lee County charges for parking at its saltwater ramps, priced by the ramp, and sells one annual pass that covers the whole county system. The launch itself is not the fee.
notes: County ramp parking runs $5 per day at Alva, Davis and Imperial River, and $10 per day at Lavender's Landing, Matlacha and Pine Island Commercial Marina. Punta Rassa, by the Sanibel Causeway, is priced by the clock: $10 for 24 hours, $20 for 48 and $30 for 72, with a 72-hour maximum stay.

The Annual Parks Parking Pass is $60 for 12 months from the date of issue. It is digital and tied to your license plate, with no sticker to display, and it is honored at the county boat ramps as well as county beach and park lots. Payment runs through Premium Parking, by app, kiosk, phone or online.

In this directory, 30 of the 71 Lee County records list a fee in the source data, running $2 to $20, and about a third of the records are run by the City of Cape Coral, whose four canal ramps follow city rules rather than the county pass.
City of Sanibel lots and the Sanibel city ramp are a separate system again, and the county pass does not cover them.

florida/monroe.intro: The Keys have no single ramp system and no single price. Monroe County, four small cities, the state parks, the state transportation department and private marinas all run launches, and in the Keys the scarce resource is not the ramp, it is legal trailer parking.
notes: Monroe County's eight county ramps are free for county residents. Visitor charges vary by ramp, and the county began adding non-resident parking and launch fees at its parks and ramps in late 2025, so expect the resident and visitor prices to differ and check the county posting for the ramp you choose.

Harry Harris Park in Tavernier is the county ramp with the clearest published visitor schedule: on weekends, non-residents pay $15 per vehicle plus a $40 boat ramp fee, rising to $15 plus $60 on holiday weekends and during the two-day lobster mini-season.

The City of Marathon runs three ramps (33rd Street, The Quay and Harbor Drive). Its published schedule lists $30 to launch, $30 to retrieve and $25 per day of trailer parking for visitors, free for Marathon and Key Colony Beach residents, and no overnight parking at any of the three.

Islamorada's Founders Park ramp is open 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.; residents launch free with ID and non-residents pay $30 each way. Small state transportation ramps such as Spanish Harbor Wayside on Big Pine Key are free for everyone, but hold only a handful of trailers.

In this directory, 27 of the 53 Monroe County records list a fee in the source data, running $4.50 to $40, the highest share of any large Florida county here, and the most common managers are private businesses and the state parks, not the county.

florida/palm-beach.intro: Palm Beach County does not charge to launch at its ramps. It charges for trailer parking, through a permit system: a daily permit bought on site, or an annual decal if you launch often.
notes: Phil Foster Park, the main ramp for the Lake Worth Lagoon and Palm Beach Inlet, requires a boat trailer parking permit, $10 per day bought on site. Jim Barry Light Harbor Park in Riviera Beach lists a $15 daily permit available on site.

Bert Winters Park and Burt Reynolds Park in Jupiter also require trailer parking permits, sold as daily permits at the ramp kiosks or as annual decals. Burt Reynolds is the county's biggest trailer lot, with about 200 spaces, and tow vehicle and trailer parking there is capped at 24 hours.

One county ramp works differently: Sunset Lake at Burt Aaronson South County Regional Park in Boca Raton requires an annual boating permit, priced for 2026 at $35 plus tax for Palm Beach County residents and $150 plus tax for out-of-county users. Hand-launched boats that do not need a trailer do not need the permit.
In this directory, 22 of the 69 Palm Beach County records list a fee in the source data, running $1.50 to $35, and 1,551 trailer spaces are recorded, close to the highest count in the state.

florida/pinellas.intro: Pinellas is a pay-to-park county: launching is not the charge, parking the tow vehicle is. The county runs pay-by-plate stations at its ramps, and regulars come out ahead with the annual pass.
notes: County boat ramp parking costs $6 per day through November 30, 2026, and rises to $12 per day on December 1, 2026. Payment is by plate at the pay station, with or without a trailer.

The Annual Boat Pass costs $140 (from October 1, 2026), with a $105 military rate and a $70 Senior Pass that also covers beach parking. The pass covers every county park boat ramp plus the Sutherland Bayou, Belleair Causeway and Park Boulevard standalone ramps, for one year from purchase.
In this directory, 24 of the 79 Pinellas records list a fee in the source data, running $2 to $12, and 1,561 trailer spaces are recorded across the county, the most of any Florida county listed here.
City ramps inside the county, including St. Petersburg's, set their own parking rules, so check the listing for the ramp you plan to use.

florida/polk.intro: Polk is freshwater lake country, and it holds more ramp records than any other Florida county in this directory: 150 of them, spread across the Kissimmee chain of lakes, the Winter Haven chain and dozens of smaller lakes. Almost all of them are free.
notes: The county, city and FWC public ramps that make up most of this list record no launch fee, including the large county parks at Saddle Creek, Lake Parker and Lake Shipp. Polk County and the FWC are the two most common managers in the records.

The fees that do appear in the Polk records, $2 to $10 across 41 listings, belong mostly to private fish camps and marinas on the Kissimmee lakes, plus the state park launch fee at Lake Kissimmee State Park. If a listing here shows a fee, check who runs it before assuming the county charges.

Trailer parking is generous by Florida standards, with 1,073 spaces recorded across the county, and the big lake ramps such as Port Hatchineha and Lake Parker carry some of the largest lots in the directory.

Polk's low water season is the winter and spring dry season: shallow lake ramps and canal launches can become unusable for larger boats until the summer rains return, which is the freshwater version of the tide problem on the coast.

florida/volusia.intro: Volusia County park ramps are free to launch from, on both sides of the county: the Halifax River and Mosquito Lagoon on the coast, and the St. Johns River and Lake George in the west.
notes: The county lists free boat ramps at Highbridge Park in Ormond Beach, River Breeze Park in Oak Hill (a four-lane ramp on the Halifax River), Lake Dias Park near De Leon Springs, and Shell Harbor Park on Lake George, which the county highlights for free boat and kayak access.

Do not confuse ramp parking with beach parking. Volusia's paid ParkVolusia program covers the county's off-beach parking lots, where residents register for free parking and visitors pay; it is a beach lot system, not a launch fee, and it does not apply to the county park ramps above.

In this directory, 18 of the 91 Volusia records list a fee in the source data, running $1 to $20, and those are concentrated in city and marina listings rather than county parks. Volusia County is the most common manager in the records, followed by the City of Ormond Beach.
The county records 844 trailer spaces. East-side ramps serve the Mosquito Lagoon fishery, where shallow water rewards local knowledge and a rising tide.
